about: Held-out testset for the judge that reads a student's reasoning on a multiple-choice question and returns a verdict (sound, flawed or missing) plus, when flawed, a misconception label. Written after the slip fix as a blind held-out check: the author did not open the judge's prompt, its code or earlier eval results, and no question from reasoning-testset.json is reused. Every item uses a real question from the hosted question bank (curriculum class-10-physics, verified MCQs with option_misconceptions); question text, options and correct indexes are copied unchanged. Reasoning is written by hand in the short, informal style of Class 10 students, in English or Hinglish in Roman script. expectedMisconception is copied verbatim from that question's option_misconceptions when the verdict is flawed, and is null otherwise. Categories: wrong-option-sound-slip (right idea and method, a careless arithmetic, unit-conversion, sign, copying or neighbouring-option slip picks a wrong option, often one that carries a label; must be sound with no label), wrong-option-flawed (wrong answer from a misconception labelled on that question), and right-option-flawed-reasoning (right answer for a wrong reason matching one of that question's labels; checks the slip fix did not make the judge lenient). topicMisconceptions lists the distinct non-empty option_misconceptions for every topic of the curriculum.

items.question: A filament lamp carries a current of 0.2 A when the potential difference across it is 2 V, and 0.4 A when the potential difference is 6 V. What happens to the resistance of the filament between these two readings?
options: It increases from 10 ohm to 15 ohm
It decreases from 10 ohm to about 6.7 ohm
It stays at 10 ohm because the lamp obeys Ohm's law
It increases from 10 ohm to 20 ohm
items.reasoning: R = V/I for each reading. first one 2/0.2 = 10 ohm. second one 6/0.4 = 20 ohm. so resistance goes up from 10 to 20, filament gets hot
items.note: Arithmetic slip: 6/0.4 worked out as 20 instead of 15. Uses V/I on each reading, so the chosen option's label (change in V over change in I) must not be assigned.

items.question: A cell drives a steady current of 0.6 A through a lamp and then through a resistor connected in series with it. How much charge passes through the resistor in 10 s?
options: 6 C
Less than 6 C, because the lamp takes up part of the current before it reaches the resistor
items.reasoning: Q = I x t hota hai. 0.6 A matlab 600 mA, toh Q = 600 x 10 = 6000 mC, jo 0.6 C hua
items.note: Unit-conversion slip: 6000 mC turned into 0.6 C instead of 6 C. Current is multiplied by time, so the chosen option's label (forgets to multiply) must not be assigned.

items.question: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 20 cm. Where is the image?
options: 12 cm on the other side of the lens
60 cm on the same side as the object
10 cm on the other side of the lens
60 cm on the other side of the lens
items.reasoning: lens formula 1/v - 1/u = 1/f. u = -30, f = +20. 1/v = 1/20 + 1/(-30) = 1/20 - 1/30. lcm 60 so (2-3)/60 = -1/60, v = -60 cm. negative so image is on the same side as the object
items.note: Sign slip: wrote 1/20 - 1/30 as (2-3)/60 instead of (3-2)/60, so v came out as -60 cm. Lens formula and sign convention are right.

items.question: A 5 Ω resistor carries 0.4 A. What potential difference is needed to double the current?
options: 4 V
2 V, because doubling the current halves the resistance
1 V
8 V
items.reasoning: resistance same rahega 5 ohm. current double karna h toh 0.4 x 2 = 0.8 A. V = IR = 0.4 x 5 = 2 V
items.note: Copying slip: worked out the new current as 0.8 A but put the old 0.4 A into V = IR. Keeps R fixed, so the chosen option's label (resistance rises with voltage) must not be assigned.

items.question: If the current through a heater is doubled while its resistance stays the same, the heat produced in the same time becomes
options: 2 times
4 times
half
unchanged
items.reasoning: H = I^2 R t. R aur t same hai, current double hua toh 2^2 = 4, matlab heat 4 guna ho jayegi
items.note: Neighbouring-option slip: reasoning says 4 times but the option just above it (2 times) was picked. It squares the current, so the chosen option's label must not be assigned.

items.question: Resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 5 Ω are connected in series. What is the equivalent resistance?
options: 5 Ω
items.reasoning: in series we just add them, 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 ohm
items.note: Neighbouring-option slip: computed 10 ohm but picked 5 ohm, the option next to it. No label on the chosen option.

items.question: You read a book in a room lit by a lamp. Which path does light take so that you can see the page?
options: From your eye to the page and back to your eye
From your eye to the lamp, then to the page
From the page straight to the lamp
From the lamp to the page, then from the page into your eye
items.reasoning: our eyes send out light rays to the page, they hit the words and bounce back into the eye, thats how we see. the lamp just makes the room bright
items.expectedMisconception: We see because eyes send out light
items.note: Believes vision works by rays leaving the eye.

items.question: One end of a current-carrying solenoid behaves like a north pole. If the current is reversed, that end
options: stays a north pole, because the iron keeps its poles
has no pole, since the field exists only outside the coils
becomes a south pole
becomes neutral but still attracts iron
items.reasoning: andar soft iron hai, ek baar magnet ban gaya toh magnet hi rehta h. current ulta karne se bhi iron ka north north hi rahega
items.expectedMisconception: An electromagnet stays magnetised when switched off
items.note: Thinks the soft-iron core keeps its magnetism once magnetised.

items.question: A 2 ohm resistor and a 4 ohm resistor are connected in parallel across a 6 V battery of negligible internal resistance. What does a voltmeter connected across the 4 ohm resistor read?
options: 6 V
4 V
3 V
2 V
items.reasoning: 6 V dono resistors me resistance ke hisaab se batega. total 2+4 = 6 ohm, toh 4 ohm wale ko 4/6 x 6 = 4 V milega
items.expectedMisconception: splits voltage by resistance as in series
items.note: Shares the battery voltage by resistance as if the resistors were in series.

items.question: A ray of light travels obliquely from medium A, with absolute refractive index 1.5, into medium B, with absolute refractive index 2.0. What is the refractive index of B with respect to A, and how does the ray bend at the boundary?
options: 4/3, and the ray bends towards the normal
3/4, and the ray bends towards the normal
4/3, and the ray bends away from the normal
3/4, and the ray bends away from the normal
items.reasoning: n of B wrt A = nB/nA = 2/1.5 = 4/3. B has the bigger refractive index so the ray bends more, away from the normal
items.expectedMisconception: thinks larger index means bending away
items.note: Ratio is right, but thinks entering the higher-index medium bends the ray away from the normal.

items.question: Two bulbs are rated 100 W, 220 V and 60 W, 220 V. Which one has the higher resistance?
options: The 100 W bulb, because it is brighter
Both are equal, since they run on the same voltage
The 60 W bulb
It cannot be decided
items.reasoning: 100 W wala bulb zyada power leta h aur zyada bright jalta hai, matlab uska resistance zyada hai tabhi wo zyada garam hota h
items.expectedMisconception: Higher wattage bulb has higher resistance
items.note: Links higher wattage and brightness to higher resistance.

items.question: Two plane mirrors are placed at 90° to each other. A ray hits the first mirror with an angle of incidence of 40°. What is the angle of incidence at the second mirror?
items.reasoning: angle of incidence is the angle between the ray and the mirror, so the ray makes 40 deg with the first mirror and reflects at 40 deg with it too. mirrors are at 90 so in the triangle 180 - 90 - 40 = 50, so it hits the second mirror at 50 deg
items.expectedMisconception: Measures angles from the mirror surface
items.note: Right answer, but measures both angles of incidence from the mirror surface; the symmetry of the 90 degree corner hides the error.

items.question: A wire of resistance R is stretched to twice its length while its volume stays the same. What is its new resistance?
options: 2R
R, because the material is the same
4R
R/2, because the wire becomes thinner
items.reasoning: stretch karne se length double ho gayi toh resistivity bhi double ho jaati h kyunki wire lamba ho gaya. R = rho l / A, rho double aur l bhi double, toh 2 x 2 = 4R
items.note: Right answer, but gets the second factor of 2 from resistivity doubling instead of the area halving.

items.question: In a household circuit, the fuse is connected in
options: the live wire
the neutral wire
the earth wire
any wire; it does not matter
items.reasoning: fuse just has to be in series with the appliance, so in live or neutral both it would cut the current when it melts. live is the usual one so i chose live
items.expectedMisconception: Fuse can go in the neutral wire
items.note: Right answer, but believes a fuse in the neutral wire would protect just as well.

items.question: A pencil partly dipped in water looks bent at the water surface. What is the best explanation?
options: Water physically bends the pencil
Light from the immersed part bends towards the normal as it leaves water, so that part looks deeper
Light travels at the same speed in water, but reflects off the surface
Light from the immersed part bends away from the normal as it leaves water into air, so that part looks raised
items.reasoning: paani denser medium hai aur denser medium me light normal se door bend hoti h, isliye pencil ka andar wala part upar utha hua dikhta h
items.expectedMisconception: Bends away from normal in denser medium
items.note: Right answer, but says light bends away from the normal because water is the denser medium.

items.question: A lamp is connected to a cell in a simple working circuit. Which statement correctly describes the current in this circuit?
options: The current is the same all the way round the circuit, because charge flows through the lamp and returns to the cell.
Less current returns to the cell than leaves it, because the lamp uses up some of the current to make light.
Current flows out of both terminals of the cell and meets inside the lamp.
Charge is created inside the cell and destroyed inside the lamp.
items.reasoning: the cell keeps making new charge and the lamp destroys it at the same rate, so the current stays the same all the way round
items.expectedMisconception: believes charge is created and destroyed in circuits
items.note: Right answer, but thinks the cell creates charge and the lamp destroys it.
